KEY FACTS
A healthy diet helps to protect against malnutrition in all its forms, as well as noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) such as diabetes, heart disease, stroke and cancer.
Unhealthy diet and lack of physical activity are leading global risks to health.

Healthy dietary practices start early in life – breastfeeding fosters healthy growth and improves cognitive development, and may have longer term health benefits such as reducing the risk of becoming overweight or obese and developing NCDs later in life.

Energy intake (calories) should be in balance with energy expenditure. To avoid unhealthy weight gain, total fat should not exceed 30% of total energy intake (1, 2, 3). Intake of saturated fats should be less than 10% of total energy intake, and intake of trans-fats less than 1% of total energy intake, with a shift in fat consumption away from saturated fats and trans-fats to unsaturated fats (3), and towards the goal of eliminating industrially- produced trans-fats (4, 5, 6).

Limiting intake of free sugars to less than 10% of total energy intake (2, 7) is part of a healthy diet. A further reduction to less than 5% of total energy intake is suggested for additional health benefits (7).

Keeping salt intake to less than 5 g per day (equivalent to sodium intake of less than 2 g per day) helps to prevent hypertension, and reduces the risk of heart disease and stroke in the adult population (8).

WHO Member States have agreed to reduce the global population’s intake of salt by 30% by 2025; they have also agreed to halt the rise in diabetes and obesity in adults and adolescents as well as in childhood over- weight by 2025 (9, 10).
OVERVIEW
Consuming a healthy diet throughout the life-course helps to prevent malnutrition in all its forms as well as a
range of noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) and conditions. However, increased production of processed foods,
rapid urbanization and changing lifestyles have led to a shift in dietary patterns. People are now consuming
more foods high in energy, fats, free sugars and salt/sodium, and many people do not eat enough fruit, vegeta-
bles and other dietary fibre such as whole grains.
The exact make-up of a diversified, balanced and healthy diet will vary depending on individual characteristics
(e.g. age, gender, lifestyle and degree of physical activity), cultural context, locally available foods and dietary
customs. However, the basic principles of what constitutes a healthy diet remain the same.
FOR ADULTS
Fruit, vegetables, legumes (e.g. lentils and beans), nuts and whole grains (e.g. unprocessed maize, millet, oats, wheat and brown rice).
At least 400 g (i.e. five portions) of fruit and vegetables per day (2), excluding potatoes, sweet potatoes, cas- sava and other starchy roots.

Less than 10% of total energy intake from free sugars (2, 7), which is equivalent to 50 g (or about 12 level tea- spoons) for a person of healthy body weight consuming about 2000 calories per day, but ideally is less than
5% of total energy intake for additional health benefits (7). Free sugars are all sugars added to foods or drinks
by the manufacturer, cook or consumer, as well as sugars naturally present in honey, syrups, fruit juices and

Less than 30% of total energy intake from fats (1, 2, 3). Unsaturated fats (found in fish, avocado and nuts, and in sunflower, soybean, canola and olive oils) are preferable to saturated fats (found in fatty meat, butter, palm and coconut oil, cream, cheese, ghee and lard) and trans-fats of all kinds, including both industrially-produced trans-fats (found in baked and fried foods, and pre-packaged snacks and foods, such as frozen pizza, pies, cookies, biscuits, wafers, and cooking oils and spreads) and ruminant trans-fats (found in meat and dairy foods from ruminant animals, such as cows, sheep, goats and camels). It is suggested that the intake of saturated fats be reduced to less than 10% of total energy intake and trans-fats to less than 1% of total energy intake (5).
In particular, industrially-produced trans-fats are not part of a healthy diet and should be avoided (4, 6).
Less than 5 g of salt (equivalent to about one teaspoon) intake per day (8). Salt should be iodized.
FOR INFANTS AND YOUNG CHILDREN
In the first 2 years of a child’s life, optimal nutrition fosters healthy growth and improves cognitive development.
It also reduces the risk of becoming overweight or obese and developing NCDs later in life.
Advice on a healthy diet for infants and children is similar to that for adults, but the following elements are also
■Infants should be breastfed exclusively during the first 6 months of life.
■Infants should be breastfed continuously until 2 years of age and beyond.
■From 6 months of age, breast milk should be complemented with a variety of adequate, safe and nutrient- dense foods. Salt and sugars should not be added to complementary foods.

text: HOW TO PROMOTE HEALTHY DIETS
Diet evolves over time, being influenced by many social and economic factors that interact in a complex manner
to shape individual dietary patterns. These factors include income, food prices (which will affect the availability
and affordability of healthy foods), individual preferences and beliefs, cultural traditions, and geographical and
environmental aspects (including climate change). Therefore, promoting a healthy food environment – including
food systems that promote a diversified, balanced and healthy diet – requires the involvement of multiple sectors
and stakeholders, including government, and the public and private sectors.
Governments have a central role in creating a healthy food environment that enables people to adopt and main-
tain healthy dietary practices. Effective actions by policy-makers to create a healthy food environment include
Creating coherence in national policies and investment plans – including trade, food and agricultural policies
to promote a healthy diet and protect public health through:
increasing incentives for producers and retailers to grow, use and sell fresh fruit and vegetables;
reducing incentives for the food industry to continue or increase production of processed foods contain- ing high levels of saturated fats, trans-fats, free sugars and salt/sodium;
encouraging reformulation of food products to reduce the contents of saturated fats, trans-fats, free sugars and salt/sodium, with the goal of eliminating industrially-produced trans-fats);
implementing the WHO recommendations on the marketing of foods and non-alcoholic beverages to children;

establishing standards to foster healthy dietary practices through ensuring the availability of healthy, nutri- tious, safe and affordable foods in pre-schools, schools, other public institutions and the workplace;

exploring regulatory and voluntary instruments (e.g. marketing regulations and nutrition labelling poli- cies), and economic incentives or disincentives (e.g. taxation and subsidies), to promote a healthy diet; and

encouraging transnational, national and local food services and catering outlets to improve the nutritional quality of their foods – ensuring the availability and affordability of healthy choices – and review portion sizes and pricing.
Encouraging consumer demand for healthy foods and meals through:
promoting consumer awareness of a healthy diet;
developing school policies and programmes that encourage children to adopt and maintain a healthy diet;
educating children, adolescents and adults about nutrition and healthy dietary practices;
encouraging culinary skills, including in children through schools;

supporting point-of-sale information, including through nutrition labelling that ensures accurate, standard- ized and comprehensible information on nutrient contents in foods (in line with the Codex Alimentarius
Commission guidelines), with the addition of front-of-pack labelling to facilitate consumer understanding;
providing nutrition and dietary counselling at primary health-care facilities.
Promoting appropriate infant and young child feeding practices through:
implementing the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes and subsequent relevant
implementing policies and practices to promote protection of working mothers; and
promoting, protecting and supporting breastfeeding in health services and the community, including through the Baby-friendly Hospital Initiative.

text: 1.1 Adequate
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: An adequate diet is one that meets, without exceeding, nutrient requirements, specific for age,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: gender, body size and body composition, levels of physical activity, physiological states (e.g.,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: The body is unable to synthesize most essential nutrients, and therefore they must be obtained
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: from the diet. These include essential amino acids, essential fatty acids and most vitamins
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and minerals. Essential nutrients are involved in all bodily functions from growth and brain
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: development in the fetus and young infant, to organ and muscle functioning throughout life.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Inadequate intake of essential nutrients can lead to specific deficiency syndromes for single
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: nutrients (such as scurvy for vitamin C deficiency, rickets for vitamin D deficiency, goiter for iodine
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: deficiency), many of which are now uncommon in most parts of the world. However, many other
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: conditions – such as, among others, impaired growth, brain development and immune system
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: function – are affected by several causes, including multiple nutrient deficiencies.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Meeting nutrient requirements for children aged 0 to 23 months
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: is particularly important given growth and development
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and the small total quantity of foods consumed. For
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: infants 0 to 6 months of age, nutrient needs should be
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: met through exclusive breastfeeding. As of 6 months
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of age, animal source foods are a good source of high
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: quality protein and bioavailable key vitamins and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: minerals. Therefore, WHO recommends, in addition
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: to continued breastfeeding, the daily consumption
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of animal source foods, including unprocessed meat,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: fish or eggs, for children in this age group (4).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Dietary requirements have been defined by FAO and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: WHO for energy (5), proteins and amino acids (6), fats
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and fatty acids (7), vitamins and minerals (8), and many
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: countries have established values for their populations.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: These requirements include the intake levels which are likely
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: to prevent risk of deficiency and the levels that will limit the risk
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of excess. For further information, including definitions of these
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: 1.2 Balanced
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: In healthy diets, energy intake is balanced with energy requirements which vary with age, sex, levels
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of physical activity and during pregnancy and lactation (5). Healthy diets require an adequate balance
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: requirements for the amount of protein, fat and carbohydrates in the diet vary with total energy
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: intake, and thus are expressed as a proportion of energy intake from each. WHO recommendations

text: for fats and carbohydrates are among those provided in Annex 2.

heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Proteins provide the building blocks for much of the structural
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: elements of the body, such as muscle, as well as functional
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: molecules such as hormones and enzymes. To meet the body’s
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: needs, 10–15% of calories consumed per day should be from
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: protein (6). This might be slightly more during adolescence,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and for athletes, body builders and others actively building
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and/or maintaining significant amounts of muscle mass.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Consuming excessive amounts of protein however can place
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: a metabolic burden on the body, particularly the kidneys (14).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Protein can come from a mix of animal and plant sources, and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: digestibility and quality should also be considered, particularly in
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: childhood and adolescence. For adults, in some contexts, switching
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: to more plant-based sources of protein may be preferable to decrease risk of cardiometabolic
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: diseases (15). In other contexts, consumption of animal source foods is still important to favour
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Fat is an essential nutrient for proper functioning of cells in the body, and two fatty acids – linoleic
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: acid and α-linolenic acid – can only be obtained from the diet. Therefore, in adults, a minimum of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: 15–30% of calories consumed per day should be from fat (7). High intakes of fat may lead to excess
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: energy intake and limiting intake to 30% or less may help to reduce the risk of unhealthy weight
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: gain (9). Because a likely mechanism by which fat intake impacts body weight is through an
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: increased intake of calories, intakes of fat higher than 30% of calories consumed per day are
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: possible, provided that energy balance is maintained and fat quality recommendations are also
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: met. Fat consumed should be primarily unsaturated fatty acids, with 6–10% of total energy intake
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: coming from polyunsaturated fats including linoleic acid, α-linolenic acid and long chain
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: polyunsaturated fatty acids (10). Monounsaturated fatty acids from plant sources should make up
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: the remainder of fat intake, after taking into consideration the amounts of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: polyunsaturated, saturated and trans-fat consumed (see 1.3 Moderate).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Carbohydrates provide the primary energy source for the body.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: The amount of carbohydrate in the diet can vary and should
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: represent the remainder of diet after taking protein and fat into
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: account. The amount should, therefore, be 75% or less of total
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: daily calories but generally at least 45% (12). Carbohydrates
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: should come primarily from whole grains, vegetables, fruits
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and pulses, and adults should aim for at least 400 grams of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: fruits and vegetables and 25 grams or more of naturally occurring
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: dietary fibre from foods every day (12). Amounts for children and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: adolescents are scaled down from adult values based on energy intake

text: 1.3 Moderate
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: As reflected by the upper limit (see 1.1 Adequate), some nutrients are essential, but in higher
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: amounts may lead to negative health effects. Other non-essential nutrients are associated with
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: negative health effects and therefore should be consumed in moderation or excluded from the diet.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Sodium is an essential mineral but at high intakes is associated with increased
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: blood pressure (16) which can lead to cardiovascular disease. Sodium intake
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: should be restricted to 2 grams per day (corresponding to 5 grams of table
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: salt, i.e., sodium chloride) in adults and proportionately lower for children
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and adolescents based on energy intake (17). Maintaining sodium intake
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: within this limit would help maintain systolic and diastolic blood pressure of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: adults and children in healthy ranges, with a resulting decrease in the risk of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: stroke and cardiovascular events and related mortality.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Free sugars1 are not essential nutrients and intake should be restricted to less than 10% of daily
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: energy intake, with less than 5% associated with additional health benefits (13).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Reduction of free sugar consumption should be achieved without the use
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of non-sugar sweeteners, as evidence suggests that they do not help with
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: long-term weight control or reducing the risk of diet-related NCDs (18).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: No more than 10% of daily energy should come from saturated fat and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: no more than 1% from trans-fat (10). Industrially produced trans-fat (e.g.,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: partially hydrogenated oils) should not be used, and therefore any trans-fat
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: should come exclusively from meat and dairy from ruminant animals. See
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: further details on WHO recommendations in Annex 2.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Moderation refers also to the avoidance of, or moderation in the consumption of, foods that may
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: have negative health effects, particularly if consumed in high quantities. This relationship may be
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: because they are sources of nutrients to limit, such as saturated fat and free sugars, or because
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: they contain other compounds that may be detrimental to health. Two key considerations in this
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: regard are red and processed meats and highly processed or “ultra-processed” foods.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: In adults, high intakes of red meat are associated with increased risk of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: several diseases (19) and evolving evidence suggests that consumption
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: of processed red meat, even at low levels, may have negative health
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: A large and growing body of evidence suggests that consumption of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: highly processed foods described as “ultra-processed” foods (UPF)
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: by the NOVA classification scheme (NOVA classification group 4) (23)
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: is associated with negative health outcomes. These include risk of
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: premature mortality, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, overweight,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: obesity and type 2 diabetes, as well as impaired mental, respiratory and
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: gastrointestinal health (24). The term UPF refers to a wide range of foods
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and beverages with a variety of characteristics.

text: 1.4 Diverse
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Diverse diets, based on a wide variety of foods, between and within food groups, are associated with a
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: greater likelihood of meeting vitamin and mineral requirements (25–32). The only exception to this is
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: during the first six months of life when infants should receive only breastmilk.
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Distinct food groups and foods within them differ in the content and density of essential nutrients
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: and many other bioactive components (33–36). Several prospective studies have reported lower
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: mortality and diet-related NCD rates among participants with higher food group diversity (37, 38),
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: greater diversity within specific food groups (e.g., fruit and vegetables) (39) and higher species
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: diversity of whole dietary patterns (40).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Dietary diversity is, therefore, a fundamental element of healthy diets and a
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: long-standing public health principle widely accepted and advocated for
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: in food-based dietary guidelines (41), FAO and WHO’s guiding principles
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: for sustainable healthy diets (42), WHO recommendations for children
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: aged 6–23 months (4) and the technical report on healthy diet metrics
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: from WHO, FAO and UNICEF (43). It is possible for people to have a
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: sufficiently diverse diet across different ages, food environments,
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: seasons, dietary restrictions (e.g., vegetarian) or cultural preferences
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: (see In conclusion: celebrating healthy dietary patterns).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: Dietary diversity is conventionally measured by a count of food groups
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: consumed over a given reference period, with or without minimum food
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: group intake criteria (25, 44, 45). The variety of possible dietary patterns is often
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: reflected in the questionnaire. For example, Minimum Dietary Diversity for Women (MDD-W) is one
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: indicator that uses intake of food groups to reflect dietary diversity. While the 10 food groups used
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: for MDD-W are universal (e.g., “milk and milk products”), when the questionnaire is administered at
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: a local level, the food groups are populated with examples of locally available, commonly consumed
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: foods that best represent the food group (e.g., kefir in one context, camel milk in another) (27).
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: This consistent structure allows for the capture of locally relevant dietary diversity data that is
heading_path: What are healthy diets? Joint statement

text: generalizable and comparable across contexts – essential for national and global monitoring of diets.

Get started now
Eating well and having a healthy lifestyle can help us feel our best – and make a big

The Eatwell Guide shows the proportions in which different types of foods are needed to

text: How does it work?
The Eatwell Guide divides the foods and drinks we consume into five main groups. Try to
choose a variety of different foods from each of the groups to help you get the wide range of
nutrients your body needs to stay healthy and work properly.
It is important to get some fat in the diet, however, foods high in fat, salt and sugar are placed
outside of the main image as these types of foods are not essential in the diet and most of us
need to cut down on these to achieve our healthy balance. Unsaturated fats from plant
sources, for example vegetable oil or olive oil, are healthier types of fat. But remember, all
types of fat are high in energy and so should only be eaten in small amounts.
Many of the foods we eat, such as pizzas, casseroles, pasta dishes and sandwiches, are
combination foods and contain ingredients from more than one of the food groups. For these
sorts of food, you just need to work out the main ingredients and think about how these fit
with the sections on the guide. For example, if you’re having a cottage pie: the potato fits into
the yellow segment; the milk in the mashed potato fits into the blue segment, the spread in
the mashed potato fits into the purple segment, the meat, meat substitute or beans would fall
into the pink segment; the onion, carrots and peas would fit into the green segment.

Fruit and vegetables
Most people know we should be eating more fruit and veg, but many of us aren’t
eating enough. Fruit and veg should make up just over a third of the food we eat
Aim to eat at least five portions of a variety of fruit and veg each day. If you count
how many portions you’re having, it might help you increase the amount and
variety of fruit and veg you eat. Choose from fresh, frozen, canned, dried or
juiced. A portion is 80g or any of these: 1 apple, banana, pear, orange or other
similar-size fruit, 3 heaped tablespoons of vegetables, a dessert bowl of salad,
juice or smoothie (counts as a maximum of one portion a day).

Food labelling
Lots of pre-packaged foods have a food label on the front of pack which shows the nutrition
information per serving. They also refer to reference intake which tells you how much of each
nutrient should be included in the daily diet. The percentage refers to the contribution that the
product makes to the reference intake for each nutrient.
Food labels can help you to choose between foods and to pick those that are lower in
energy, fat, saturated fat, sugar and salt. Where colour coded labels are used you can tell at a
glance if they are high, medium or low in fat, saturated fat, sugars and salt. For a healthier
choice, try to pick products with more greens and ambers and fewer reds.

Cutting down on saturated fat

Cutting down on saturated fat can lower your blood cholesterol and reduce your risk of heart
disease. Most people in the UK eat too much saturated fat. The average man should have no
more than 30g saturated fat a day. The average woman should have no more than 20g
saturated fat a day. Children should have less saturated fat than adults. But remember that a
low-fat diet isn’t suitable for children under five.
One of the easiest ways to cut down on saturated fat is to compare the labels on similar
products and choose the one lower in saturated fat. Watch out for foods that are high in
saturated fat, including fatty cuts of meat, sausages, butter, cream, cheese, chocolate,
pastries, cakes and biscuits. You don’t need to stop eating these foods altogether, but eating
too much of these can make it easy to have more than the recommended maximum amount
of saturated fat. To find out more, see www.nhs.uk/Livewell/Goodfood/Pages/Eat-less-
Cutting down on sugar
Regularly consuming foods and drinks high in sugar increases your risk of obesity and tooth
decay. Ideally, no more than 5% of the energy we consume should come from free sugars*.
Currently, children and adults across the UK are consuming 2-3 times that amount.

| Age | Recommended maximum free sugars intake | Sugar cubes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4-6 years | No more than 19g/day | 5 cubes |
| 7-10 years | No more than 24g/day | 6 cubes |
| From 11 years, including adults | No more than 30g/day | 7 cubes |
Many packaged foods and drinks contain surprisingly high amounts of free sugars* including
some breakfast cereals, yoghurts and fruit juice drinks. Use the food label to help you choose
foods lower in sugar. Swap sugary breakfast cereals for plain cereals such as plain porridge,
wholewheat biscuit cereals, shredded wholewheat or no added sugar muesli. Cereal bars
often contain high levels of free sugars* too, so remember to check the label. Swap flavoured
or corner-style yoghurts for low fat, lower sugar yoghurts, adding fresh fruit for variety.
*Free sugars - Any sugar added to food or drink products by the manufacturer, cook or
consumer including those naturally found in honey, syrups and unsweetened fruit juice.
Sugary drinks have no place in a child’s daily diet but account for a surprisingly large proportion
of the daily sugar intake of both children and adults. Almost a third of the free sugars consumed
by 11-18 year olds comes from soft drinks. We should aim to swap sugary drinks for water,
lower fat milk or sugar-free drinks including tea and coffee. Be sure to check the label for added
sugar. For more information, visit www.nhs.uk/Livewell/Goodfood/Pages/sugars.aspx.
Cutting down on salt
Eating too much salt can raise your blood pressure, which increases your risk of developing
heart disease or stroke. And since many people in the UK eat too much salt, that means that
lots of people would benefit from cutting down. Adults should eat no more than 6g of salt a
day. Children should have even less. 6g of salt is about a teaspoonful. But remember we’re
not just talking about the salt you add to your food because most of the salt we eat is already
in everyday foods such as bread, breakfast cereal, pasta sauce and soup. Try replacing salt
with pepper, herbs and spices to add flavour to your favourite dishes. Checking the label and
choosing foods that are lower in salt is one of the best ways to cut down. For more
information, visit www.nhs.uk/Livewell/Goodfood/Pages/salt.aspx.

text: Chilling, freezing and defrosting food properly helps stop harmful bacteria from growing.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Here are our top recommendations on chilling and freezing your food safely:
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: your fridge should be between 0 and 5°C and your freezer should be around -18°C
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: keep chilled food out of the fridge for the shortest time possible during preparation (a maximum of four hours)
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: eat leftovers within two days or freeze if you think this won’t be possible
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: 1. Chilling food
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Your fridge should be set between 0 and 5°C. Using a fridge thermometer is the best way to do this and we would recommend checking once a week.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: To make sure your fridge is running safely you can use the built-in dial or gauge inside the fridge to change the power setting. Check the manufacturer’s instructions on how to do this correctly.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: You should always store any food with a ‘use by’ date, as well as cooked dishes, salads and dairy products, in your fridge. Follow storage instructions on packaging, including the best before and use-by dates .
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Keep chilled food out of the fridge for the shortest time possible during preparation (a maximum of four hours). And don’t leave the fridge door open for long periods of time, as your fridge then has to work harder to lower the temperature.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Don’t place hot or warm food in your fridge. Instead, cool cooked food at room temperature and place in the fridge within one to two hours. To cool food quickly, divide food into smaller portions in containers or freezer bags before putting in the fridge or freezer.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Leftovers can be eaten cold if they have been cooked properly, cooled, and put in the fridge within two hours. Putting food in the fridge slows bacterial growth so it is safe to eat. Eat leftovers within 48 hours or freeze them if you think this won’t be possible. For more information see the ‘Using your leftovers’ section on our ‘ Cooking your food ’ page.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: 2. Freezing Food
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: A freezer acts as a pause button - food in a freezer won’t go bad and most bacteria cannot grow in it. It’s OK to freeze most foods as long as you check packet instructions to ensure that foods are suitable for freezing.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Here’s our top tips on freezing your food safely:
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: your freezer should be around -18°C
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: follow any freezing or defrosting instructions on the label
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: you can freeze food right up until midnight on the ‘use by’ date printed on the label
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: leftovers and homemade goods should be frozen as soon as possible
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: cool any warm dishes before putting them in your freezer
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: to cool food quickly, divide food into smaller portions in containers or freezer bags before putting in the freezer
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: To stop the cold air in your freezer from drying out your food (known as freezer burn) you should:
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: place food in an air-tight container
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: wrap it well in freezer bags or freezer wrap
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: label food you freeze so you don’t end up with Unidentified Frozen Objects (UFOs)
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: FSA Explains: Freezer burn Freezer burn is when foods in the freezer are exposed to cold, dry air, which causes them to dehydrate and form ice crystals over time. This process affects the quality of the foods, rather than the safety. Freezer burn can be avoided by carefully packaging foods in the freezer and checking foods aren’t kept for too long. Meats are usually best eaten within 2-3 months. Baked goods, fruit and veg are best between 3-4 months. Love Food Hate Waste have information on freezing leftovers, including recipe ideas.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: 3. Defrosting Food
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: You should defrost your food in the fridge so that it doesn’t get too warm, see our Danger Zone info below for why this is important. It’s also important to use food within 24 hours after it’s been fully defrosted – it will go bad in the same way as if it were fresh.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: When defrosting your food, make sure it has been fully defrosted and that the middle (and most dense bit of the food) is fully thawed. Partially defrosted food may not cook evenly and this means that harmful bacteria could survive the cooking process.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: When defrosting food in the fridge use a container big enough to catch any drips. If this isn’t possible, use a microwave on the defrost setting directly before cooking. Check the guidance on food packaging and allow enough time for your food to defrost properly.
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: Other things to remember when defrosting your food:
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: always clean surfaces, chopping boards, utensils, plates and hands thoroughly with warm soapy water after they have touched raw or thawing meat to stop bacteria spreading around the kitchen
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: you can freeze food again once cooked, but you’ll only be able to reheat it once after that
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: freezing in individual portions will help you defrost only what you need
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: we also have tips on defrosting a Christmas turkey and other large cuts of meat
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: 4. How to stock your fridge
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: It’s especially important to store meat, fish and poultry safely to stop bacteria from spreading and to avoid food poisoning:
heading_path: How to chill, freeze and defrost food safely

text: store raw meat, poultry and fish in their packaging or in clean sealed containers on the bottom shelf of the fridge, so they can’t touch or drip onto other food

text: FSA Explains: The Danger Zone The cold temperatures of a domestic freezer (-18°C) delay chemical reactions within foods and put any bacteria that may be present on pause. The bacteria haven’t been killed, and they may be revived as the food defrosts. Defrost food in the fridge to prevent it sitting in between 8 - 63°C, which is the Danger Zone. Between these temperatures the bacteria may grow and make you ill. Generally, the colder the temperature, the slower bacteria will grow - but cold temperatures don’t stop bacteria growing altogether (for example, listeria monocytogenes ). text: Power Outages
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Keep an appliance thermometer in both the refrigerator and freezer. Make sure the refrigerator temperature is at
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: 40 °F (4.44 °C) or below and the freezer
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Keep the freezer full. Fill empty spaces with frozen plastic jugs of water, bags of ice, or gel packs.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Keep the refrigerator and freezer doors closed to keep cold air inside.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: The refrigerator will keep food safe for up to 4 hours. If the power is off longer, you can transfer food to a cooler and fill with ice or frozen gel packs. Make sure there is enough ice to keep food in the cooler at 40 °F or below. Add more ice to the cooler as it begins to melt.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: If your freezer is not full, group packages so they form an “igloo” to protect each other.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: For longer power outages, add dry ice or cubed or block ice.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: During a snowstorm, do not place perishable food out in the snow. food can be exposed to unsanitary conditions and animals. The sun’s rays can thaw frozen food. Instead, make ice in containers left outside to freeze. Then put the “homemade ice” in your refrigerator, freezer, or coolers.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: In general, refrigerated items should be safe up to 4 hours.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Discard any perishable food that has been above 40 °F (4.44 °C) for 2 hours or more. (See Focus on: The Danger Zone on page 9.) unusual odor, color, or texture, or feels warm to the touch. Never taste a food to determine its safety!
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: With frozen food: check for ice crystals! The food in your freezer that partially or completely thaws before power is restored may be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is 40 °F (4.44 °C) or below.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: A full freezer will stay at safe temperatures about 2 days; a half-full freezer about 1 day. refrigerator will not keep foods frozen as long.

text: When the power comes back on, you will have to evaluate each item separately. When in doubt, throw it out.

text: Do not eat any food that may have come into contact with flood water.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Discard any food that is not in a waterproof container if there is any chance that it has come into contact with flood water. Food containers that are not waterproof include those with screw-caps, snap lids, pull tops, and crimped caps. Also discard cardboard juice/milk/baby formula boxes and home-canned foods if they have come in contact with flood water, because they cannot be effectively sanitized.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Inspect canned food and discard any food in damaged cans. Can damage is shown by swelling, leakage, punctures, holes, fractures, extensive deep rusting, or crushing/denting severe enough to prevent normal stacking or opening with a manual, wheel-type can opener.
heading_path: Kitchen Companion: Your Safe Food Handbook

text: Undamaged, commercially prepared foods in all-metal cans and retort pouches (e.g., flexible, shelf- stable juice or seafood pouches) can be saved if the can is properly cleaned and treated.
